text: Busbie Castle was located in what is now Knockentiber (Scottish Gaelic: Cnoc an Tobair, hill of the well), a village in East Ayrshire, Parish of Kilmaurs, Scotland. Knockentiber lies 2 miles (3.2 km) WNW of Kilmarnock and 1/2 mile NE of Crosshouse. The castle overlooked the Carmel Glen and its Burn, which flows into the River Irvine, a mile or so to the south, after passing through the old Busbie Mill. Ainslie's map of 1822 labels the settlement as Bushby, while Armstrong's map of 1775 shows Busbie Castle in a ruinous state but still with its old woodland policies. The 1860s first edition of the Ordnance Survey (OS) indicates a pre-reformation chapel dedicated to the Virgin Mary was situated near the castle site. A small hamlet of thatched cottages was clustered nearby; in 1860, the OS shows 'Old Busbie' on the opposite side of the road from the castle. Over time, Busbie and Knockentiber grew together. The castle was a simple keep, approximately 50 feet (15 m) high and about 40 feet (12 m) long by 25 feet (7.6 m) wide. Its entrance was on the ground floor, leading to a wheel-stair to the first-floor hall in the north-west angle and to two cellars or stores on the ground floor. The first-floor hall featured a large fireplace and two window seats. Historical records from the Registrum Magni Sigilli in 1465 list "Terras de le Moite," and in 1539, "9 marcat. de Busby, viz., lie Mote, Knokintibber, et Hallethornis," and in 1541, "Terras de Moite, Knokintebir," and in 1571, "Terras de Moit," and in 1583, "20 solidatas terrarum antiqui extentus de Moit-Mowat cum earum mansione," and in 1599, "9 marcat. terrarum de Busbeyis (viz., lie Mote, Knockiutibber et Halythornis)." In 1691, the Laird of Busbie's dwelling had six hearths and seven other dwellings were associated with the castle and its lands. The castle was a ruin since at least the 1770s and was demolished in 1949 or 1952 due to safety concerns and lack of funds to consolidate it. H. Ritchie built Busbie House as a replacement. Busbie Estates and Collective Securities Limited owned significant land in the 1950s. MacIntosh in 1894 describes the castle as a "prominent object in an otherwise monotonous landscape," noting gun ports, arrow slits, and a sculptured cable winding fantastically around the walls. He claims the castle likely had three floors, was roofless and in decay, and dates it to the 14th century, possibly built by the Mowat family from Flintshire in the 12th century. A Robert de Montealt is recorded in Scotland during the time of King David I; later, several soldiers with that name led armies into Scotland. William Craufurd of Wallston married a daughter of Mowat of Busbie around 1400. Charles Mowat of Busbie is mentioned in 1534 for involvement in the murder of William Cunyngham of Craganis and his servant; he was tutor to Hugh, Earl of Eglinton in 1546 and fined £47 in 1571–2 for celebrating mass at Eglinton Castle. In 1547, Charles Mowat was involved in the murder of Lord Boyd, with Sir Neil Montgomerie of Lainshaw as the victim; he was required to remain in France until Sir Neil Montgomerie’s son allowed him to return. A brother of the Earl of Eglinton appeared in court for provoking John Mowatt, Laird of Busby, and his servant Andrew Stevenston in Stewarton. The Mowat involved in the Montgomerie murder was later killed by William and Harrie (Sic) Stewart, sons of Lord Ochiltree, in 1577. Alexander, the eldest son, did not inherit; instead, James, his younger brother, succeeded to the Busbie lands. James’s son, also named James, is the last Mowat to appear in public records. The name de Monhaud or de Monte Alto is recorded as being pronounced 'Mowat' by Dalrymple. James Ritchie of Craigton obtained the lands in 1763, succeeded by his son Henry in 1799, who also acquired the Cloncaird estate. William Wallace of Cairnhill (now Carnell), the nephew of Henry, next inherited the estate. General Sir James Wallace died in 1867 and passed the property to William Wallace of Busbie and Cloncaird. In 1661, Hugh, Earl of Eglinton inherited the lands of Busbie, Knockentiber, and Robertown, a family holding these lands as far back as 1638. The barony, formerly part of the Barony of Kilmaurs, extended from Kilmaurs south to the River Irvine. It had no manor house and was later held by the Eglinton family. Hugh Montgomerie, 1st Earl of Eglinton, received a charter on 3 February 1499 from James V for the £40 lands of old extent of Roberton in Cunninghame. These lands were part of the Lands and Barony of Ardrossan, which included parts of Kilmaurs, Knockentiber, Craig, Gatehead, Woodhills, Greenhill, Altonhill, Plann, Hayside, Thorntoun, Rash-hill Park, Milton, Windyedge, Fardelhill, Muirfields, and Corsehouse. The present Busbie farm appears on older maps, such as the 1860 OS, as a mill with a clear millrace or lade and a sluice. The water was drawn from the Carmel near a dwelling marked as Busbie Holm, rejoining the burn just beyond the mill. The exact date when the mill ceased operation is unclear. It is likely the mill was associated with the castle and the Lairds of Busbie. A Robertown mill is known to have existed, named after the barony.
